'''Robert Johnson Omohundro''' (June 21, 1921 – May 15, 2000) was a nuclear physicist who contributed to [[Manhattan Project|The Manhattan Project's]] efforts in the atomic bomb development during [[World War II]]. Omohundro's notable work included aiding in the creation of radiation detection devices, portable neutron detectors, and holding patents for scintillation counters and selective detectors for fission neutrons.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=2024-01-10 |title=OBITUARIES |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/2000/05/20/obituaries/db2659e0-23da-463e-8994-b5bf45478328/ |access-date=2024-04-04 |newspaper=Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Robert Johnson Omohundro was born on June 21, 1921, in [[Norfolk, Virginia]], to Henry Omohundro and Brownie Pierce Omohundro.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robert Omohundro in the 1940 Census {{!}} Ancestry® |url=https://www.ancestry.com/1940-census/usa/Virginia/Robert-Omohundro_m88s0 |access-date=2024-04-04 |website=Ancestry.com |language=en}}</ref> He had a younger sister named Gladice and four half-siblings, Joseph, Mildred, Annie Mae, and Dorothy.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Absher |first=A. |date=2011-11-14 |title=Robert Johnson Omohundro (1921-2000) |url=https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/omohundro-robert-johnson-1921-2000/ |access-date=2024-04-04 |website=Black Past |language=en-US}}</ref>

Omohundro graduated from [[Booker T. Washington High School (Virginia)|Booker T. Washington high school]] in his hometown then went to work for the Western Electric Company as a radio tester.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Colvin |first=Leonard E. |date=2023-08-18 |title=Norfolk "Unsung Hero" Instrumental In Developing WWII Atomic Bomb |url=https://thenewjournalandguide.com/norfolk-unsung-hero-instrumental-in-developing-wwii-atomic-bomb/ |access-date=2024-04-11 |website=The New Journal and Guide |language=en}}</ref> Later, he earned a bachelor’s degree in mathematics and a master’s in physics from [[Howard University]] in Washington, D.C.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Sluby |first=Patricia Carter |url=http://archive.org/details/inventivespirito0000slub |title=The inventive spirit of African Americans : patented ingenuity |date=2004 |publisher=Westport, Conn. : Praeger |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-275-96674-4 |pages=113}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Scott |title=Robert Johnson Omohundro |url=http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/physics/omohundro_robertjohnson.html |access-date=2024-04-16 |website=Physicists of the African Diaspora}}</ref> He was also a member of the [[Alpha Phi Alpha]] fraternity,<ref name=":4" /> which is the oldest and largest African American fraternity and made huge contributions to the fight for African Americans' civil rights.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Our History |url=https://apa1906.net/our-history/ |access-date=2024-04-11 |website=Alpha Phi Alpha |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Career ==
Robert Johnson Omohundro was a research nuclear physicist for the [[Naval Research Laboratory]] in Washington.<ref name=":0" /> He worked at the laboratory from 1948 to 1984 for 36 years.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /> Some of his most notable work included being a part of the [[Manhattan Project]] where he helped develop the atomic bomb, created instruments for measuring, and identified radiation emissions coming from nuclear warheads.<ref name=":3" /> He also developed a satellite-based system to detect vacuum ultraviolet radiation and a mass spectrometer carried by rockets for studying in the upper atmosphere.<ref name=":0" /> Additionally, he worked on airport screening devices to identify fissionable materials and portable neutron detectors supplied to the [[International Atomic Energy Agency]] to prevent plutonium proliferation.<ref name=":0" /> Along with his work on the projects, Omohundro received two patents in nuclear physics and contributed as an author or co-author to over 40 scientific articles.<ref name=":1" /> During his time working on the Manhattan Project, he was subjected to keeping everything done on the job a secret.<ref name=":1" /> While being part of the Manhattan Project during World War II, he worked on a secret test facility located in Arizona. The secret test facility worked on developing devices to locate radiation emissions.<ref name=":1" />

Omohundro lived to be 78 years old and died of cardiac arrest on May 15, 2000 in the Washington University hospital.<ref name=":0" />
